reason: The sources provide detailed accounts of the collection mishap, scientific findings, and specific recovery data supported by at least two independent sites.
story: In 2020, NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft attempted a high-stakes 'fist-bump' with the carbon-rich asteroid Bennu to collect a surface sample. Using a burst of nitrogen gas, the probe’s TAGSAM arm successfully stirred up rocks and dust, but it was too successful. The collector head grabbed so much material that large pebbles jammed the internal mylar seal open. Mission control watched in horror through onboard cameras as precious bits of the asteroid drifted away into the vacuum of space. Fearing the entire sample might leak out, NASA scrapped plans to weigh the material and rushed to stow the container in its return capsule days early. When the capsule finally landed in Utah in 2023, scientists found 121.6 grams of material—more than double their original goal. This pristine haul contained water-altered minerals and the chemical building blocks of life, including amino acids and the essential components of DNA.
angle: The OSIRIS-REx spacecraft collected so much of asteroid Bennu that the sampler's lid jammed open, causing the prehistoric cargo to leak into space before NASA could rush it into a storage capsule.

claims.claim: OSIRIS-REx launched on September 8, 2016, from Cape Canaveral.
The spacecraft’s target was the carbon-rich near-Earth asteroid 101955 Bennu.
The mission was built by Lockheed Martin Space Systems.
The primary sample collection site on Bennu was a northern crater named Nightingale.
On October 20, 2020, the spacecraft touched down on Bennu to collect a sample.
The TAGSAM instrument used a burst of nitrogen gas to blow surface particles into the sampler head.
Large rocks jammed the sampler's mylar seal flap open after the collection event.
Images from the spacecraft showed flakes of the asteroid sample escaping into space.
NASA canceled a spinning maneuver to measure the sample mass to prevent further loss of material.
The mission team expedited the storage procedure, stowing the sample days earlier than originally planned.
The sample return capsule landed in the Utah desert on September 24, 2023.
The total recovered mass of the Bennu sample was 121.6 grams (4.29 ounces).
The amount collected was more than double the mission's minimum requirement of 60 grams.
The returned sample contains a wide range of organic compounds, including 14 different amino acids.
The sample contains the nucleobases that are essential building blocks of DNA and RNA.
The asteroid material contains a nearly equal mix of left-handed and right-handed amino acids.
Following the sample delivery, the spacecraft was renamed OSIRIS-APEX for a new mission to asteroid Apophis.

disputed: The exact number of nucleobases found is described as 'four' by some sources (S1) and 'all 5' by others (S4); the script should refer to them generally as the essential building blocks of DNA and RNA.
The biological model for the Egyptian deity Bennu is debated as being either a heron or a kingfisher; the script should treat this as mythological background.
